orders.explanation: Transcript 1 is from the more capable model. It correctly identifies the root cause in Django’s migration `EnumSerializer`, implements a robust fix (serializing by enum member name), updates all affected tests including secondary breakages (e.g., `re.RegexFlag` as an `IntEnum`), adds documentation, and validates via targeted repro plus running relevant test suites. Transcript 2 makes a less careful serializer change (dropping needed imports handling), struggles to execute Django’s test harness properly, and produces cascading unrelated test failures without resolving them.

Transcript 2 identifies the precise root cause in `EnumSerializer`, implements a clean fix (serializing by `Enum.name` and emitting `EnumClass['NAME']`), and then correctly updates the impacted expectations in the migration writer tests, including the subtle knock-on effect for `re.RegexFlag` (an `IntEnum`). It also demonstrates the bug scenario with a round-trip example and verifies the fix by running the relevant Django test suites. Transcript 1, by contrast, applies a brittle patch, struggles to run the test suite correctly, and ends with multiple failing tests and unresolved issues, indicating weaker debugging and integration capability.

Transcript 1 shows stronger debugging and codebase navigation: it quickly locates the exact behavioral change in `_save_table()`, traces it to the known Django tickets/commits (#29260/#31071), and applies the minimal correct fix (`not raw`) that preserves the optimization while restoring fixture/loaddata behavior. Transcript 2 confirms the bug via a reproducer, but proposes an incorrect logic change that breaks an existing regression test and then gets stuck exploring deeper refactors without reaching a correct patch.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it quickly zeroes in on the relevant logic in `Model._save_table()`, connects the reported regression to the known upstream fix for ticket #31071, and applies the minimal, targeted patch (`not raw`) that preserves the #29260 optimization while fixing fixture/loaddata behavior. Transcript 1 does good reproduction and debugging, but proposes an incorrect condition based on “pk explicitly set” that fails existing tests due to UUID defaults being populated during `__init__`, and it doesn’t reach a correct final patch.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger debugging and engineering rigor: it reproduces the failure within Django’s own test framework, identifies the precise root cause in `_delete_composed_index()`, finds the upstream fix (including commit reference), applies it cleanly, and adds/updates targeted regression tests, then validates by running relevant test suites. Transcript 2 does reach the same code change, but it relies on ad‑hoc scripts, hits an avoidable app-label setup error, uses a brittle `sed` edit, and doesn’t add robust regression tests or broader validation. The breadth of investigation and quality of verification in Transcript 1 indicate the more capable model.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it not only reproduces the bug but also traces it to an existing upstream fix (commit 533b208775), cleanly applies the patch, and validates it by running the relevant Django test suites. It additionally updates/extends regression tests in the correct locations (migrations test base + operations) and verifies broader test coverage, demonstrating stronger engineering rigor than Transcript 1’s ad-hoc local script and direct sed edit without a proper regression test.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it implements a minimal, targeted fix in `QuerySet.in_bulk()` using the existing `opts.total_unique_constraints`, correctly limiting acceptance to unconditional single-field `UniqueConstraint`s (matching the ticket’s intent). It also adds proper regression tests (including negative cases for conditional and multi-field constraints) and updates documentation/release notes, then runs relevant Django test suites to validate. Transcript 2 makes a broader, riskier change by adding a new `Options.unique_fields` API and doesn’t integrate a proper regression test into Django’s test suite or update docs, indicating weaker judgment and completeness.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it implements a minimal, well-scoped fix directly in `QuerySet.in_bulk()` using the existing `_meta.total_unique_constraints`, and it adds comprehensive regression tests (including negative cases for conditional and multi-field constraints) plus documentation/release note updates. It also runs and reports relevant Django test suites to validate the change. Transcript 1 introduces a new `Options.unique_fields` cached property (a broader API surface change) and doesn’t add upstream-style tests or docs, making it a less precise and less complete solution.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it locates and applies the exact upstream fix (deduplicating locations via `sorted(set(...))`), adds an appropriate regression test to the project’s test suite, updates the changelog, and validates the fix with a before/after reproduction. It also preserves determinism (sorted output) and avoids altering UUID semantics, whereas Transcript 2’s approach drops UUIDs for duplicate locations and doesn’t add an in-repo regression test, risking behavioral changes when `gettext_uuid` is enabled.

Transcript 2 is the more capable response because it identifies the exact upstream Sphinx fix for this known issue, applies the minimal correct code change (deduplicating locations with a deterministic order), and adds an explicit regression test plus a CHANGES entry. It also validates the behavior with a concrete repro showing the before/after duplication count. Transcript 1’s fix is reasonable but is noisier, doesn’t add a regression test, and changes UUID handling in a way that goes beyond the established upstream solution.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a much stronger end-to-end engineering approach: it finds the precise option parsing and filtering locations, reuses existing `members_option` semantics (including `ALL`), updates both module and class documenters, adds targeted regression tests, updates documentation and CHANGES, and verifies edge cases like `autodoc_default_options` and negated options. Transcript 2 makes a workable core change but does so redundantly (introducing a new option function instead of reusing the existing one), adds no repository tests/docs updates, and shows difficulty validating the behavior (broken ad-hoc testing and a failing conf.py). Overall, Transcript 1 shows higher competence in codebase integration, testing discipline, and product-quality completion.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it implements the feature with minimal, idiomatic changes (reusing `members_option` for `private-members`), updates the filtering logic appropriately, and then adds/adjusts documentation, changelog, and a solid set of automated tests (including config default/negation edge cases). It also diagnoses unrelated pre-existing test failures via stashing and compares behavior, showing stronger debugging hygiene. Transcript 1 is less complete (no doc/changelog updates, incomplete testing, and some ad‑hoc patching/manual testing errors).

Transcript 1 is more capable because it quickly isolates the true root cause (splitting the typed `:param` field at the first whitespace), finds the upstream fixing commit, applies the minimal correct change (`split` → `rsplit`), and adds an appropriate regression test plus a CHANGES entry. It also validates the fix by running relevant test suites and distinguishes unrelated pre-existing failures. Transcript 2 meanders, repeatedly breaks the file while attempting an overcomplicated helper parser, and ends without adding proper regression coverage or a clean, minimal patch.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it quickly pinpoints the true root cause in Sphinx’s `DocFieldTransformer` (splitting the `:param type name:` field at the wrong whitespace), then finds and applies the exact upstream fix (`split` → `rsplit`) with minimal, correct code change. It also adds an appropriate regression test and CHANGES entry, and validates the fix across relevant test suites while correctly identifying an unrelated pre-existing failure. Transcript 1 eventually reaches a working fix, but does so via a more error-prone, overly complex custom parser and multiple failed patch attempts, with weaker test/regression coverage.

Transcript 1 is markedly more capable because it sets up the full, correct end-to-end system the prompt requires: an SSH-accessible Git remote (`user@server:/git/server`) plus an auto-deploy mechanism to a webroot served on port 8080. It anticipates and fixes real operational issues (no `sudo`, permissions on `/git` and `/var/www`, lack of systemd, service startup, correct `HEAD`/branch handling), validates via an actual SSH push and curl, and leaves reusable documentation. Transcript 2 largely bypasses the SSH requirement (no `openssh-server`/`sshd`, tests via local filesystem clone), provides a weaker deploy hook, and leaves a partially broken webroot behavior (403 at `/`).

Transcript 2 is more capable because it sets up the full end-to-end system implied by the user’s commands: a real SSH-accessible Git repo (`user@server:/git/server`), an appropriate deploy hook, and an nginx server on port 8080, plus service startup in a non-systemd container. It also handles environment issues correctly (no `sudo`, permissions/ownership, SSH host keys) and validates via an actual SSH-based clone/push workflow. Transcript 1 largely works locally but omits SSH server/user setup and leaves a less production-accurate configuration (e.g., initial 403, root-owned repo), making it less robust and less aligned with the requested interface.

Transcript 1 shows substantially stronger investigative and debugging ability: it discovers that the `default` and `metadata` configs are not aligned, determines that the `default` split is entirely code-only, and correctly infers that “science domain” must be taken from `metadata` (physics/chemistry/biology per README). It also validates tokenizer behavior (no special tokens), cross-checks counts via multiple equivalent methods (including batch tokenization), and resolves the concatenation discrepancy with a principled separator check. Transcript 2 reaches the right number but includes a flawed “tokenize concatenated fields” verification that produces an inconsistent total, only later asserting the per-example sum is correct without as deep a justification.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it performs deeper validation and resolves key ambiguities: it discovers the `default` and `metadata` configs are not row-aligned and that `default` contains only code prompts, confirming the science-domain DeepSeek fields must come from `metadata`. It also rigorously checks tokenizer behavior (special tokens), compares multiple token-counting methods, and explains the concatenation-boundary discrepancy, including a batch-tokenization cross-check, making the final count far more defensible.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger troubleshooting and systems competence: it correctly diagnoses missing dependencies (Perl LZMA module, missing 7z tools), handles a CPU instruction-set mismatch (AVX2-required John build on an AVX-only CPU) by rebuilding John with the appropriate SIMD target, and proceeds with an efficient, standard cracking workflow. Transcript 2 is more trial-and-error, installs an incompatible “john” (no 7z support), resorts to an inefficient brute-force loop via Python/7z, and triggers avoidable interactive package configuration (tzdata), indicating weaker planning and tool awareness.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it follows a clearer diagnostic workflow, chooses the most direct dependency fix (installing `libcompress-raw-lzma-perl` via apt instead of struggling with CPAN), and correctly identifies/handles the AVX2 CPU incompatibility by rebuilding John with AVX support. Transcript 1 succeeds but is significantly more error-prone and inefficient (attempts a long source build that times out, installs an incompatible distro `john` lacking 7z support, then falls back to a custom Python brute-force loop after extra installs and friction). Overall, Transcript 2 demonstrates better system reasoning, tool selection, and recovery from environment constraints.

Transcript 1 is the more capable response because it performs a deeper, end-to-end root-cause analysis (including inspecting the in-house libstdc++ patches, confirming header/library mismatch behavior, and using gdb to pinpoint when facet registration occurs). It then implements a robust fix that works even if the internal registration symbol is absent (weak symbol + independent stream-based triggers), and validates correctness with repeated runs, output-diff checks, and careful Valgrind interpretation (including proving the “still reachable” block is pre-existing). Transcript 2 reaches a working fix but with a more superficial investigation and less robustness/verification.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it performs a deeper, more rigorous investigation: it inspects the in-house libstdc++ patches in `/build/`, confirms the exact crash path with gdb, and identifies the patched facet-registration/destruction mechanism that differs between debug and release builds. It then designs a robust fix (including a weak-symbol call plus independent stream-based triggers) and validates behavior with repeated runs, gdb, and Valgrind, ensuring the solution is resilient to linkage/header nuances. Transcript 1 reaches a working fix, but it relies on a higher-level hypothesis and doesn’t leverage the available `/build/` evidence or confirm the specific patched behavior.

Transcript 1 shows substantially deeper cryptanalytic understanding and engineering maturity: it derives and verifies the probability‑1 differentials, correctly exploits the ciphertext-to-last-round state relation, and explicitly analyzes/handles the kernel-induced equivalent-key ambiguity and why the 16‑bit seed schedule resolves it. It also includes extensive reliability/timing testing, edge-case checks, and careful implementation details (e.g., private RNG, early-exit checks), resulting in a robust solution aligned with the task constraints. Transcript 2 reaches a working solution but with more trial-and-error, less rigorous handling of subtleties (like equivalent-key structure), and fewer robustness considerations.

Transcript 2 demonstrates substantially stronger cryptanalytic reasoning and engineering rigor: it verifies probability‑1 differentials formally/numerically, derives and checks ciphertext-to-round-state relations, identifies the kernel/equivalent-key ambiguity intrinsic to the round function, and justifies why the 16‑bit seed schedule makes key[5] uniquely recoverable. It also builds and tests multiple characteristic families, adds sanity checks, isolates RNG state, and runs broad reliability/timing evaluations. Transcript 1 reaches a working solution, but with less theoretical justification and fewer robustness considerations (and some earlier confusion before settling on the correct approach).

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it correctly localized the failure to header handling, identified the precise weakness as CRLF injection (CWE-93), implemented the minimal, appropriate fix (_hkey/_hval validation raising ValueError), generated a correctly formatted report.jsonl, and verified the full test suite passes. Transcript 2 is less capable: it initially overreaches by adding an unrelated CWE-502 report, uses inconsistent CWE formatting, applies broad risky changes (attempting to remove pickle usage) that break existing tests, and ends in an incomplete/unstable state.

Transcript 2 is the more capable response because it quickly triangulates the root cause via the failing test, correctly maps it to CWE-93 (CRLF injection), applies the minimal targeted fix in `_hkey`/`_hval` to raise a specific `ValueError`, and verifies the full test suite passes. Transcript 1 is significantly less disciplined: it overreaches into unrelated “pickle” issues (CWE-502), introduces breaking behavioral changes, and shows a confused/debugging-heavy workflow that would risk correctness and scope creep. Transcript 2 also produces the required `report.jsonl` with the exact relevant file and CWE id and keeps changes aligned with upstream behavior.

Transcript 1 demonstrates substantially stronger systems competence: it discovers key environment constraints (no systemd), configures sshd/nginx accordingly, designs a fast, synchronous deployment hook using `git archive` with atomic directory swaps, and validates timing and end-to-end behavior repeatedly from a pristine state. It also proactively addresses common pitfalls (safe.directory, permissions on `/var/www`, known_hosts seeding, TLS SANs, nginx alias quirks) and leaves the repo clean for grading. Transcript 2 reaches a working state but only after multiple missteps (wrong default branch, missing rsync, host-key failures, broken nginx mapping/permissions, manual deployment intervention) and shows less robust, less deterministic setup.

Transcript 2 is clearly produced by the more capable model: it systematically inspects the environment (noting no systemd), sets up sshd/nginx in a container-appropriate way, uses a fast and atomic `git archive | tar` deployment that reliably meets the 3-second requirement, and explicitly handles host key trust to avoid interactive prompts. It also diagnoses and fixes a real permission issue in the hook deployment path, then re-tests from a pristine state to mirror the grader flow, demonstrating stronger robustness and operational awareness than Transcript 1’s trial-and-error path with multiple misconfigurations and missing dependencies.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it anticipates and handles environment constraints (missing `ps`, `ss`, `netstat`), generates and validates the gRPC code carefully (including the hyphen→underscore module-name sanitization), and starts the server robustly in a truly detached background process with logging and persistence checks. It also performs stronger verification, including independent stub generation and compatibility testing, and avoids introducing a `package` in the proto that could change service names/paths and break an external checker. Transcript 2 is more brittle (adds `package kvstore;`, uses a simple `&` background launch, and lacks reliable process/port inspection), making it less generally correct and less robust.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it proactively inspects and adapts to the environment (e.g., missing `ps`, `ss/netstat`), uses a more reliable background launch (`setsid nohup`) with logging, and performs extensive verification including independent stub generation and wire-compatibility checks. It also anticipates potential pitfalls around hyphenated proto filenames/module names and validates imports and descriptor behavior. Transcript 1 completes the task but is less robust and performs only minimal validation with some failed tooling checks.

Transcript 1 delivers a genuinely optimized solution by writing and integrating a custom C extension tailored to the “dominant eigenpair only” requirement, with certification logic and robust fallbacks; it achieves large, consistent speedups over NumPy across sizes while maintaining correctness guarantees. Transcript 2 mostly swaps in SciPy’s `eig` (plus a 2×2 shortcut), which yields only modest and sometimes inconsistent speed improvements and adds a heavyweight dependency without fundamentally reducing the computational work. Transcript 1 also demonstrates deeper debugging, performance profiling, and robustness engineering (build-at-import, embedded source).

Transcript 2 is markedly more capable because it develops and validates a specialized C extension that avoids computing the full eigendecomposition, adds certification and safe fallbacks, and even ensures deployability by supporting build-at-import and embedding the C source. It performs extensive correctness and dominance testing (random, structured, adversarial) and demonstrates large, consistent speedups over the numpy reference across all matrix sizes. Transcript 1 explores alternatives but ultimately relies on SciPy/NumPy routines with marginal or inconsistent performance gains and far less engineering rigor.

Transcript 1 demonstrates substantially deeper understanding and optimization of the provided cost model: it derives closed-form decode costs, identifies the true p95 indexing behavior, and builds a constrained merge-based optimizer that explicitly manages padding and p95 while also optimizing the global shape set jointly across buckets. It achieves better margins with fewer shapes (5 vs. 8) and includes extensive constraint/performance validation and reproducibility checks. Transcript 2 reaches passing metrics, but relies on a relatively simple heuristic (fixed shape ladder + gen_len range batching), shows more trial-and-error, and does not exploit key model properties (e.g., p95 floor, compile/shape coupling) as effectively.

Transcript 2 demonstrates substantially stronger capability: it deeply reverse-engineers the cost model (including the exact p95 indexing behavior), builds and iteratively debugs a principled constrained optimizer (with explicit handling of pad/p95/compile costs), and then jointly optimizes the global shape set across both buckets—reducing unique shapes to 5 while improving margins. It also performs more comprehensive validation (reproducibility, constraint checks, robustness to percentile conventions) and achieves better overall efficiency than the simpler heuristic in Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a much stronger end-to-end systems capability: it correctly configures Mailman3 + Postfix LMTP integration, handles Postfix’s recipient validation edge case for `-confirm+token` addresses via a regexp in `local_recipient_maps`, starts the right processes, and validates the setup with the provided `/app/eval.py` (and additional flow checks). Transcript 2 repeatedly misconfigures Postfix (breaking local delivery and mailbox format expectations), struggles with Mailman shell automation, and ultimately introduces extra packages (procmail) to patch delivery—while leaving `mailman.cfg` largely at defaults (e.g., `site_owner` unchanged). Overall, Transcript 1 is more systematic, technically accurate, and robust.

Transcript 2 shows a clearer understanding of Mailman3/Postfix LMTP integration and proactively handles tricky edge cases (e.g., `reading-group-confirm+TOKEN@local.edu` recipient validation) with a proper Postfix `regexp:` local recipient map rather than ad‑hoc workarounds. It also makes more principled configuration choices (minimal package changes, correct use of Mailman-generated transport maps, and disabling the unnecessary NNTP runner) and demonstrates stronger debugging methodology (reading Mailman source, enabling Postfix logging). Transcript 1 reaches a working state but via much more trial-and-error, including installing `procmail` and repeatedly reworking Postfix delivery settings, indicating weaker diagnosis and design.

Transcript 1 shows stronger end-to-end capability: it diagnoses missing tooling, installs dependencies cleanly, inspects bundle refs, fetches both branches from HEAD, performs and validates a true merge commit, and then rigorously deduces the transformation by checking hypotheses programmatically against all examples. Its final `algo.py` is also more robust/generalized (infers the stripe period from observed diagonals, avoids numpy, preserves a compatible alias), and it performs thorough repo hygiene and verification (fsck, conflict-marker scan, clean status). Transcript 2 reaches a passing solution for the visible examples but hard-codes the modulo-3 assumption and has weaker generalization and verification rigor.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only completes the required git operations and merge, but also performs deeper diagnostics and produces a more robust final solution. It correctly deduces the transformation, fixes both branches’ conceptual bugs, and implements a generalized period-detection approach (rather than hard-coding `% 3`), while also validating repo health (merge parents, conflict-marker scan, fsck, clean working tree) and maintaining backward compatibility (`transform` alias). Transcript 1 succeeds on the given examples but is less thorough and less general in its implementation and verification.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it iteratively diagnoses and fixes real polyglot pitfalls (e.g., GCC lexer warnings from unbalanced triple quotes), verifies both execution paths, and upgrades the C implementation to arbitrary-precision arithmetic so it matches Python for large N (beyond 64-bit overflow). It also adds robust, consistent argument parsing and error handling in both languages and checks clean builds under strict warning flags. Transcript 2 works for small inputs but silently overflows for moderate N, has weaker input validation, and doesn’t ensure parity with Python’s big-integer behavior.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only produces a working Python/C polyglot, but also iteratively diagnoses and fixes issues (initial GCC warnings from the triple quotes), verifies behavior under stricter compiler flags, and ensures correctness parity between Python’s big integers and C by implementing arbitrary-precision arithmetic on the C side. It performs extensive cross-check testing across large N and improves input validation, demonstrating stronger engineering rigor and robustness than Transcript 1’s simpler 64-bit-only C implementation.

Transcript 1 shows substantially deeper competence: it diagnoses performance bottlenecks (CPU thread oversubscription), empirically evaluates prompting strategies against available polyline “GT,” develops principled mask-selection heuristics, implements overlap resolution and contiguity/hole handling, and even adds robust large-image tiling/cropping logic with extensive validation. Transcript 2 is comparatively simplistic (box-only prompting, global score-based overlap arbitration, minimal post-processing) and lacks many robustness considerations (selection quality, hole filling, component enforcement, large-image handling), even if it happens to work on the demo.

Transcript 2 demonstrates substantially stronger engineering capability: it iteratively prototypes, measures runtime, tunes CPU threading, evaluates prompt/selection strategies quantitatively (IoU), and hardens the pipeline with overlap/contiguity guarantees plus large-image tiling support. It also performs systematic debugging when regressions appear (e.g., self-conflict bug in polygon finalization) and adds multiple edge-case tests (missing type column, bad coords, large images). Transcript 1 is comparatively straightforward and works on the demo, but relies on a simplistic “highest-score pixel assignment” overlap rule that can fragment masks and lacks the same depth of validation, robustness, and performance tuning.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it not only writes a correct SPARQL query but also rigorously validates it end-to-end by installing the needed tooling, executing the query against the actual TTL data, and checking edge cases (graduation/enrollment date boundaries) and portability across two SPARQL engines. It demonstrates deeper ontology/data inspection, careful handling of “currently enrolled,” and correct aggregation of all work-country values while enforcing existence constraints via subqueries/EXISTS. Transcript 2 produces a plausible query but never successfully runs or verifies it, and its logic is less robust (e.g., full-professor detection only excludes “Assistant Professor,” and enrollment-date handling requires that property to exist).

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only derives a correct SPARQL query but also rigorously validates it end-to-end by installing missing tooling, executing the query against the actual TTL with two independent SPARQL engines (rdflib and pyoxigraph), and running targeted diagnostic and boundary-condition tests to confirm the “currently enrolled” and “>10 students” logic. It also uses `FILTER EXISTS` and careful grouping to ensure the country aggregation is not accidentally restricted by the qualification constraints, and it documents assumptions clearly. Transcript 1 arrives at a correct query but does not execute it, has a less robust role filter, and relies mainly on manual reasoning after encountering missing tooling.

Transcript 1 shows substantially stronger capability: it profiles where time is spent, systematically explores solver/jacobian combinations, validates numerical equivalence across many seeds, and explicitly rejects tempting but incorrect speed hacks (e.g., disabling contact) after finding a counterexample seed that would fail correctness. It then implements a minimal, robust MJCF change (`jacobian="dense"` + carefully tuned PGS tolerance/iterations) and re-verifies both speed and correctness repeatedly. Transcript 2 reaches a passing configuration but does so with more trial-and-error, less rigorous robustness checking, and a narrower optimization (solver switch only) that is more likely to be brittle across hidden tests.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it uses systematic profiling and controlled experiments to identify where runtime is spent (factorizations, Jacobian mode, solver choice), then validates candidate changes against both accuracy and speed across many seeds. It also anticipates hidden correctness pitfalls (e.g., rare but real contact events) and explicitly tests/discards tempting speed hacks like disabling contacts that would fail on some seeds. Transcript 1 reaches a working solution, but with more trial-and-error, weaker justification, and less robust coverage of edge cases.
